content.text: You’ve made it to the end of the seventh part of this series, so let’s summarize:

numbered: You can create your own types using structures, which can have their own properties and methods.
You can use stored properties or use computed properties to calculate values on the fly.
If you want to change a property inside a method, you must mark it as `mutating`.
Initializers are special methods that create structs. You get a memberwise initializer by default, but if you create your own you must give all properties a value.
Use the `self` constant to refer to the current instance of a struct inside a method.
The `lazy` keyword tells Swift to create properties only when they are first used.
You can share properties and methods across all instances of a struct using the `static` keyword.
Access control lets you restrict what code can use properties and methods.

title: Structs: Summary
question: Which of these are true about structs?
hint: Structs let us group together properties and methods, and are used very commonly in Swift.

correct.answer: Structs can have as many or as few properties as you need.

correct.reason: Custom initializers usually replace the default memberwise initialiser.

correct.answer: Strings and arrays are both structs.
Methods that change properties must be marked `mutating`
correct.reason: Swift won't let you change a struct's properties unless you mark the method as mutating.

correct.answer: You can share properties and methods across all instances of a struct using `static`
Computed properties let us run code to return a value.

wrong.answer: A struct may either have stored properties or computed properties, but not both.
wrong.reason: You can mix and match the two however you want.

wrong.answer: Structs may not use constant properties.
wrong.reason: Constant properties work just fine with structs.

wrong.answer: The `filepublic` access level allows us to modify a property from anywhere in our program.
wrong.reason: There is no such access level.

wrong.answer: The `self` keyword must not be used inside initializers.
wrong.reason: You can use `self` freely in initializers.

wrong.answer: You must always write your own initializer for structs.
wrong.reason: You can rely on Swift's default memberwise initializer a lot of the time.
They can use lazy properties just fine.
